user_prompt: What is the effect of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) interventions, delivered alone or combined with exercise (e.g. a cognitive-behavioural or multicomponent programme such as "A Matter of Balance", behaviour-change/motivational support, Tai Chi plus CBT), compared with control (usual care, no intervention, or an attention/discussion/education control), on fear of falling in community-dwelling older people, measured immediately after the intervention?  Effect measure: pool as a standardised mean difference (SMD, Hedges' g) using a random-effects model. SMD < 0 means less fear of falling in the intervention arm (favours intervention).  Outcome: fear of falling / falls-related self-efficacy, extracted as the post-intervention mean, SD and number of participants per arm. - Scale direction: on FES-I and similar concern scales a higher score means more fear; on confidence scales (e.g. FES-S, mFES, ABC) a higher score means more confidence/less fear. Reverse the sign of confidence scales (multiply by −1) so that a lower value always means less fear before computing the SMD. - If a study reports several fear-of-falling measures, use one per study in this order of preference: FES-I (and its short form), then modified FES / FES / Swedish FES-S / ABC, then a single-item fear question. - Use the first assessment after the intervention ended, within about one month of its end where possible. If a study only reports later follow-ups, use the earliest one. Do not use the 6-month or longer follow-up when an earlier post-intervention value exists. - Use post-intervention scores rather than change scores when both are reported. - Multi-arm trials: include every arm that has a CBT or behaviour-change component (CBT only, CBT with exercise, CBT with Tai Chi, exercise with motivational interviewing). Exclude exercise-only arms with no behavioural component. If two eligible arms share one control group, divide the control group's sample size equally between the comparisons so the control participants are not counted twice. - Cluster-randomised trials: use the cluster-adjusted results when the paper reports them; if the paper ignores clustering, reduce the sample sizes accordingly and state the adjustment. - Multiple reports of the same trial: extract once. Use the short-term or primary report for the post-intervention timepoint.  Do not pool follow-up timepoints beyond the first post-intervention assessment, activity avoidance, depression, anxiety, quality of life, falls count, or adverse events. Include only randomised trials in people aged 60 or over living in the community. Exclude exercise-only, education-only, home-modification or hip-protector interventions with no CBT component.
